claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys can be engineered to exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Hierarchically patterned microstructures and coherent phase interfaces enable the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The engineered interfaces avoid conventional temper-embrittlement mechanisms.
The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy is strong yet brittle.
The starting alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
High-pressure and high-temperature treatment modifies the EHEA microstructure.
Thermal cycling and controlled HPHT processing induce changes in deformation mechanisms across a specific temperature window.
HPHT treatment forms a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces.
The HPHT-induced microstructure promotes dislocations, stacking faults, microbands, and deformation twins at multiple length scales.
The HPHT-induced microstructure relieves stress concentration at interfaces and arrests interfacial cracking.
Relieving interface stress concentration mitigates brittle fracture associated with temper embrittlement.
Temperature-dependent adjustment of the dominant deformation mechanisms causes behavior to change from ductile to brittle and back to ductile.
The processed alloy will have high ductility at low and high temperatures but reduced ductility at intermediate temperatures.
The width and magnitude of the ductile–brittle–ductile transition can be tuned through processing parameters.
Conventional alloys, including tungsten-based heavy alloys, typically undergo temper embrittlement within a narrow temperature window.
Comparable temper embrittlement has not been reported in compositionally complex high-entropy alloys.
The proposed effect should extend to EHEAs with similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures.
The proposed effect may depend on alloy composition and HPHT processing parameters.
The precise transition-temperature range and quantitative ductility change are uncertain.
Failure to observe a reproducible intermediate-temperature region of reduced ductility after HPHT treatment would falsify the proposed transition.
